# Crypto Lab — algorithm catalog

<!-- catalog-sync:begin — generated by tools/catalog-sync.js from the cards in index.html; do not edit by hand -->

Every line below is generated from `index.html`, which stays the single source of
truth. The algorithm facts on each card are derived from that lab's own source by
`tools/catalog-evidence.js`, and each implemented algorithm carries the `file:line`
where the evidence is. Source shapes the scanner cannot establish are recorded
in `tools/catalog-reviewed.json` at a pinned lab commit. Nothing here is edited by hand.

**Implemented** means the lab's code computes it — the algorithm appears in a
declaration, an invocation, a module import, a WebCrypto call, or a pinned source review.
**Referenced** means the lab names it without implementing it: a lab that teaches an
attack on HQC by modelling its decode time references HQC without implementing HQC.
The distinction is the point of the index, and a grep cannot make it.

Regenerate with `node tools/catalog-sync.js`; re-derive the underlying facts with
`node tools/catalog-evidence.js write`; re-check every anchor against the lab clones
with `node tools/catalog-evidence.js verify`.

## Overlap report

Pairs of labs that implement the same algorithms, weighted so that sharing a rare
algorithm counts and sharing SHA-256 does not. An overlap is not a fault — two labs
may teach the same primitive from different angles — but an overlap **with no stated
difference** is a question nobody has answered, and a visitor choosing between the
two has nothing to go on.

86 pairs: 7 with a stated difference, **1 examined and found to be duplication**, 78 nobody has looked at.

A pair marked DUPLICATION is a finding, not a description: someone read both and
found no difference worth having. It is listed first because it is the only row here
that asks for a decision.

**Babel Hash / Hash Zoo**

- **Shared:** BLAKE3, SHA-256, SHA-3
- **Stated difference:** **DUPLICATION** — both compare the same three hash functions (SHA-256 Merkle-Damgard, SHA3-256 sponge, BLAKE3 tree) and both compute every digest in-browser from the real primitives. The only separation the two READMEs support is that babel-hash sits in the crypto-compare portfolio, which is where a lab lives rather than what it teaches. Needs a decision on whether one absorbs the other, not a sentence.

**HPKE Envelope / Blind Relay**

- **Shared:** ChaCha20, ChaCha20-Poly1305, DHKEM, HKDF, HPKE, Poly1305, SHA-256
- **Stated difference:** **none stated**

**SNARK Arena / Polynomial Forge**

- **Shared:** Groth16, KZG commitment
- **Stated difference:** **none stated**

**Frodo Vault / Scloud+ Vault**

- **Shared:** FrodoKEM, LWE, ML-KEM
- **Stated difference:** both are unstructured-LWE KEMs: frodo-vault is FrodoKEM, the conservative plain-LWE design that avoids algebraic structure outright; scloud-vault is Scloud+, which keeps unstructured LWE but adds ternary secrets and Barnes-Wall lattice coding for efficiency

**KDF Chain / KDF Arena**

- **Shared:** Argon2, HKDF, PBKDF2, scrypt, SHA-256
- **Stated difference:** kdf-chain teaches what problem each KDF solves and walks a decision tree for choosing one; kdf-arena benchmarks the same four side by side and reports attacker cost against wall-clock time

**FROST Threshold / Shamir vs FROST**

- **Shared:** Ed25519, FROST, SHA-512, Shamir secret sharing
- **Stated difference:** **none stated**

**Ratchet Wire / Encrochat**

- **Shared:** AES, AES-GCM, Diffie-Hellman, Double Ratchet, HKDF, SHA-256, X25519
- **Stated difference:** ratchet-wire demonstrates the Double Ratchet working as designed; encrochat reconstructs the 2020 Encrochat takedown, where the same construction was never broken and the endpoint was compromised instead

**STARK Tower / Polynomial Forge**

- **Shared:** FRI, Merkle tree, SHA-256
- **Stated difference:** stark-tower runs a whole STARK, prover and verifier, catching a cheating prover through a FRI low-degree test; polynomial-forge opens the commitment layer underneath and compares KZG, IPA and FRI as schemes in their own right

**Format Ward / Regex Veil — FTE**

- **Shared:** AES, AES-CBC, FF1
- **Stated difference:** format-ward PRESERVES an existing format with FF1 and FF3-1, so ciphertext keeps the length and alphabet of the input; fte TRANSFORMS ciphertext into whatever language a regular expression defines, by ranking a DFA slice

**VSS Gate / Reshare Circle**

- **Shared:** Feldman VSS, Pedersen commitment, Shamir secret sharing
- **Stated difference:** vss-gate adds VERIFIABILITY to Shamir sharing at deal time, through Feldman and Pedersen commitments; reshare-circle leaves the dealing alone and refreshes shares over time, using HJKY proactive sharing against perpetual leakage

**Blind Hello / Blind Relay**

- **Stated difference:** **none stated**

## Labs

225 labs. Implementation findings and source coverage are separate questions.

**N/A (4)** — source-reviewed labs that model an attack or
system but implement no named algorithm in this index. N/A is a reviewed
finding, not the automatic scanner's answer to a miss.

**UNKNOWN (0)** — every file this scanner reads was read and no algorithm was
derivable, with no source review resolving whether that is an intentional model or
a missed implementation. Do not treat this as N/A.

**NOT-SCANNED (0)** — the lab implements its cryptography in a language this
scanner does not read, so there is no finding either way. `could not look` is not
`nothing there`, and collapsing the two would publish "implements nothing" about source
nobody opened.

**Partially unread (5)** — some bundled source or binary remains opaque
to this index; the algorithm list is a floor rather than a total.

### Ablation Wire

[`crypto-lab-ablation-wire`](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-ablation-wire/) · Layer Ablation · PROTOCOLS, ATTACKS, POST-QUANTUM

The 1942 Navajo code-talker stack rebuilt on modern primitives, with every layer independently switchable — turn one off and discover which was actually load-bearing.

- **Implements:** AES-GCM `codetalker-core/src/aead.rs:5`, ChaCha20-Poly1305 `codetalker-core/src/aead.rs:6`, Ed25519 `codetalker-core/src/identity.rs:172`, HKDF `codetalker-core/src/kdf.rs:4`, ML-DSA `codetalker-core/src/identity.rs:221`, ML-KEM `codetalker-core/src/kem.rs:253`, SHA-256 `codetalker-core/src/kdf.rs:5`, X25519 `codetalker-core/src/kem.rs:97`
- **Source review:** [8ad03c068a13](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-ablation-wire/commit/8ad03c068a133660b27755ff0910e0391f8e0dcc) — Rust crypto core reviewed; WASM is built from that core
- **References:** AES, ChaCha20, DHKEM, Diffie-Hellman, Double Ratchet, EC point arithmetic, Pairing, Poly1305
- **Attacks shown:** Discrete log `TEACHING.md:243`, Known-plaintext attack `README.md:298`, Man-in-the-middle `web/index.html:2493`, Nonce reuse `web/index.html:1344`, Side-channel (unspecified) `README.md:278`
- **Standards body:** IETF, NIST
- **Implementation:** Rust crates / WASM

### Adaptor Gate

[`crypto-lab-adaptor-gate`](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-adaptor-gate/) · Scriptless Scripts · SIGNATURES, PROTOCOLS

One click turns a pre-signature the real BIP-340 verifier rejects into a valid signature, then subtracts the two to read the secret back out — the fact that atomic swaps and PTLC routing are both built on.

- **Implements:** Schnorr `src/crypto/attacks.ts:8`, secp256k1 `src/crypto/adaptor.ts:156`, SHA-256 `src/crypto/vectors.ts:23`
- **Source review:** [f838c41a6708](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-adaptor-gate/commit/f838c41a6708ee52e70e395f394c53b513d31558) — secp256k1 is added by review because the scanner now reads `import { schnorr } from '@noble/curves/secp256k1.js'` as a module path rather than an implementation, which is right in general and wrong here: src/crypto/secp.ts wraps that import into the lab's own point and scalar layer (N, G, mulG, mul, liftX, invModN) and src/crypto/adaptor.ts computes the adaptor construction on it directly. The anchor is the defining point addition, R + T, not the import. Adaptor layer is the lab's own code over @noble/curves point/scalar ops; the completed signature is verified by the library's unmodified BIP-340 verify. Ledgers and PTLC routing are modeled and labelled as such in-page; PTLC settlement is causal (each hop consumes the value extracted downstream), not precomputed.
- **References:** EC point arithmetic, ECDSA, FROST
- **Attacks shown:** Discrete log `src/ui/honesty.ts:109`, Key recovery `src/ui/honesty.ts:50`, Nonce reuse `src/crypto/attacks.ts:65`
- **Standards body:** NIST, SECG
- **Implementation:** @noble

### Collision Vault

[`crypto-lab-collision-vault`](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-collision-vault/) · Hash Collisions · HASHING & KDFS, ATTACKS

- **Source review:** [476dec52aa83](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-collision-vault/commit/476dec52aa83e9eb3045cfb79a6e01d9a030f0d0) — The lab hashes with WebCrypto through one local helper, and names the algorithm only as that helper's STRING ARGUMENT: hashing/index.ts:79 is `return webcryptoDigest('SHA-256', bytes)` and :81 the SHA-512 case, while webcrypto.ts:25 does the work as `subtle().digest(algo, copy)` with algo a parameter. No line carries both the name and the operation, so no detection shape can reach it, and the only other place either name appears in executable code is a vectors table (SHA256_VECTORS, SHA512_VECTORS) - which is test data, not an implementation, and is now correctly suppressed. Reviewed by reading hashing/index.ts and hashing/webcrypto.ts in full: both digests are computed by the platform on the learner's input, which is the lab's whole subject. Anchored at the call sites rather than at the digest call, because those are the lines that say WHICH algorithm.
- **References:** BLAKE3, CMAC, GHASH, HMAC, Keccak, Kupyna, Merkle tree, Poly1305, Streebog
- **Attacks shown:** Birthday bound `README.md:62`, Brute force `demos/collision-vault/src/pairs/manifest.ts:64`, Collision attack `demos/collision-vault/src/hashing/index.ts:44`, Length extension `demos/collision-vault/src/main.ts:214`
- **Standards body:** IETF, NIST

### Function Key

[`crypto-lab-function-key`](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-function-key/) · Functional Encryption · ENCRYPTION

Issue a key that answers one question about an encrypted vector — its weighted sum — and nothing else. Then issue keys one at a time and watch the set of possible plaintexts shrink, until one more key hands over the master secret.

- **Implements:** ABDP15 IPFE `src/crypto/attacks.ts:24`, Baby-step giant-step `src/crypto/dlog.ts:130`, EC point arithmetic `src/crypto/ristretto.ts:80`, ristretto255 `src/crypto/dlog.ts:25`, SHA-512 `src/crypto/prng.ts:47`
- **Source review:** [f6628c00c2b7](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-function-key/commit/f6628c00c2b70ddde2efd7462f0b9494e8c00d7d) — Browser TypeScript throughout, no other language and no WASM. Group operations are @noble/curves 2.4.0, pinned to RFC 9496 Appendix A (16 A.1 multiples both directions, 29 A.2 rejections, 8 A.3 map outputs) before any scheme code was written on it; ABDP15 Construction 3.1 and the baby-step giant-step, exact-rational and mod-l algebra are implemented in-repo. Five derived attacks are removed because none is an attack this lab shows, and each was matched by a different accident: Man-in-the-middle came from the string 'DH MITM' inside CATALOG-ENTRY.md, which is this catalog's own concept line quoted back in the lab's handoff doc and not lab source at all; Signature malleability from /malleab/i on a seed label, in a lab that has no signatures - what it demonstrates is CIPHERTEXT malleability, and its own source calls that 'not an attack and not a flaw in the proof'; Chosen-plaintext attack from CPA inside 'IND-FE-CPA', the security notion ABDP15 proves rather than an attack mounted; Chosen-ciphertext attack from CCA inside 'Any CCA security whatever', a line in the NOT-BUILT list; and Discrete log from 'baby step', which this lab pays as a decryption cost and never mounts. The two attacks it does show, key collusion and ciphertext malleability, have no term in the vocabulary. Baby-step giant-step is added by review: src/crypto/dlog.ts is a baby-step giant-step over a symmetric range, but it names the algorithm only in comments and in the local counters babySteps and giantSteps, and the exported function is called dlogSymmetric. The anchor is that function, not the counter a narrower shape used to read.
- **References:** BLS signatures, BLS12-381, CKKS, Ed25519, ElGamal, FROST, Hash-to-curve, LWE, MD5, Paillier, RSA, SHA-256, Schnorr, Shamir secret sharing, X3DH

- **Standards body:** IETF, NIST

ChaCha20 is HAND-ROLLED here rather than imported, because it is the teaching subject and a reader has to be able to open the file: the scanner anchored it at src/crypto/pinned.ts:18, which is that file's import line, so the pin moves it to the block function it actually implements. AES-GCM and SHA-256 come from crypto.subtle and their anchors are the real call sites. The lab's point is that a generator seeded from a guessable value produces guessable keys while every check on the page still reports success -- the key from a four-digit PIN is rebuilt by trying ten thousand seeds, which is counting rather than cryptanalysis.

### HTTPS Padlock

[`crypto-lab-https-padlock`](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-https-padlock/) · What the Padlock Means · PROTOCOLS, SIGNATURES

Takes apart a certificate a real site presented, lets you break each of its four checks in turn, then shows a flawless certificate for a lookalike domain that passes every one. Reads captured certificates; it never connects to a site.

- **Implements:** ECDSA `src/pki/path.ts:86`, X25519 `src/tls/clienthello.ts:282`
- **Source review:** [28ad74791a7e](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-https-padlock/commit/28ad74791a7e904c41b74508c814189fbdbf33f2) — Read src/pki/path.ts, parse.ts, assess.ts, break.ts and src/tls/clienthello.ts. The scanner found only X25519 in the ClientHello builder. The chain walk really does verify every signature: src/pki/path.ts:86 calls @peculiar/x509's verify with the parent's public key and the WebCrypto provider, over real DER TBS bytes, and the certificates this lab ships are ECDSA over P-256 and P-384 -- so ECDSA is pinned above. Scope that the card and chips are written to respect: the lab makes NO network connection and runs no handshake, so it never observes encryption; it reads certificates captured earlier. Its RFC 5280 path validation is a stated teaching subset, deliberately omitting revocation, name constraints, policy constraints and path length, so a chain this page accepts is not thereby a chain a browser would accept. The ClientHello is encoded byte for byte and never sent, and its X25519 private half is discarded unused -- which is why the chip is marked 'ClientHello Bytes Only' rather than claiming TLS 1.3. Trust terminates in the lab's own committed copy of a root list, not the reader's device trust store, and the page says so.
- **References:** ChaCha20, ChaCha20-Poly1305, ECDH, Encrypted Client Hello, P-256, P-384, Poly1305, RSA, SHA-256, SHA-384, TLS 1.3
- **Standards body:** IETF, NIST
- **Implementation:** WebCrypto

### Locks and Keys

[`crypto-lab-locks-and-keys`](https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-locks-and-keys/) · Public-Key Basics · ENCRYPTION, SIGNATURES

A padlock anyone may close and only you can open &mdash; real RSA-OAEP and RSA-PSS on a 2048-bit pair, with the wrong key failing on purpose and the same pair doing its other job, signing. No maths on screen.

- **Implements:** RSA `src/crypto/lock.ts:40`, RSA-OAEP `src/crypto/pinned.ts:42`, RSA-PSS `src/crypto/pinned.ts:57`, SHA-256 `src/crypto/pair.ts:35`
- **Source review:** [6b23b1fa6cde](https://github.com/systemslibrarian/crypto-lab-locks-and-keys/commit/6b23b1fa6cde4f39c3f20a6e0468da2c913eb430) — Read src/crypto/pair.ts, lock.ts, sign.ts, vectors.ts, pinned.ts and vectors.test.ts. One 2048-bit RSA pair does two different jobs: RSAES-OAEP encryption and RSASSA-PSS signing. The page is careful that signing is NOT encryption run backwards, and the scanner's RSA / RSA-OAEP / RSA-PSS / SHA-256 anchors are the real WebCrypto call sites. Two negative claims are carried in the lab rather than implied: a successful decryption establishes nothing about WHO encrypted the message, since anyone holding the public half could have; and a verifying signature ties a note to a KEY, not to a person. Correctness rests on 12 pinned Project Wycheproof cases -- 6 OAEP and 6 PSS, of which 4 must be REFUSED -- taken from rsa_oaep_2048_sha256_mgf1sha256_test.json and rsa_pss_2048_sha256_mgf1_32_test.json and run in the reader's own browser. RFC 8017 is cited for the SCHEMES only (§7.1 RSAES-OAEP, §8.1 RSASSA-PSS) and never for the numbers, because RFC 8017 publishes no test data; src/crypto/vectors.test.ts asserts that attribution cannot drift. The build brief's claim of 'a pinned RSA-OAEP / RSA-PSS vector from RFC 8017's test data' was wrong and is corrected in audits/BRIEF-locks-and-keys.md.
- **References:** Ed25519, HPKE, ML-KEM, P-256, Schnorr, TLS 1.3
- **Standards body:** IETF, NIST
- **Implementation:** WebCrypto
